name: Phoenix and Beauty
description: Phoenix loves beautiful arrays. An array is beautiful if all its subarrays of length $$$k$$$ have the same sum. A subarray of an array is any sequence of consecutive elements. Phoenix currently has an array $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$. He wants to insert some number of integers, possibly zero, into his array such that it becomes beautiful. The inserted integers must be between $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$ inclusive. Integers may be inserted anywhere (even before the first or after the last element), and he is not trying to minimize the number of inserted integers.
input_specification: The input consists of multiple test cases. The first line contains an integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 50$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le n \le 100$$$). The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ space-separated integers ($$$1 \le a_i \le n$$$) — the array that Phoenix currently has. This array may or may not be already beautiful.
output_specification: For each test case, if it is impossible to create a beautiful array, print -1 . Otherwise, print two lines. The first line should contain the length of the beautiful array $$$m$$$ ($$$n \le m \le 10^4$$$). You don't need to minimize $$$m$$$. The second line should contain $$$m$$$ space-separated integers ($$$1 \le b_i \le n$$$) — a beautiful array that Phoenix can obtain after inserting some, possibly zero, integers into his array $$$a$$$. You may print integers that weren't originally in array $$$a$$$. If there are multiple solutions, print any. It's guaranteed that if we can make array $$$a$$$ beautiful, we can always make it with resulting length no more than $$$10^4$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1348B — Phoenix and Beauty [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
